reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the chapter as describing two distinct sets of twelve stones — one carried out and set up at Gilgal, one left standing in the riverbed.

discrepancy.connective: The Hebraist Benjamin Kennicott argued the riverbed memorial "flatly contradicts the rest of the chapter," holding the text corrupt and emending "in the midst" to "from the midst" so that only the single Gilgal set was meant.

skeptic.name: Benjamin Kennicott
skeptic.work: The State of the Printed Hebrew Text of the Old Testament Considered (Dissertation the First)
skeptic.attribution: Benjamin Kennicott (d. 1783), The State of the Printed Hebrew Text of the Old Testament Considered, Dissertation the First (1753)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It seems from this chapter that there were two sets of stones erected as a memorial of this great event; twelve at Gilgal, Jos 4:20 and twelve in the bed of Jordan, Jos 4:9. The twelve stones in the bed of Jordan might have been so placed on a base of strong stone-work so high as always to be visible, and serve to mark the very spot where the priests stood with the ark.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly resolves the 4:9-vs-4:20 tension by asserting two separate sets of twelve stones (Gilgal set + riverbed set) and explaining how the riverbed set stayed visible 'unto this day' — the strongest, most explicit harmonization on the row.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Joshua 4:9
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this specific passage at length, defending the two-sets-of-stones reading against Kennicott's emendation and concluding no textual change is needed.
